thesis.company_overview:
Encompass Health Corporation (NYSE: EHC) is the largest owner-operator of inpatient rehabilitation hospitals in the United States, providing post-acute rehabilitative care — intensive physical, occupational and speech therapy — to patients recovering from stroke, traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injury, neurological disorders and orthopedic procedures. Revenue is generated predominantly from Medicare and Medicare Advantage, supplemented by commercial payers and Medicaid, with demand driven by an ageing US population, rising neurological and stroke incidence, and the migration of higher-acuity recovery out of short-stay acute-care hospitals. The growth model is a self-funded de novo development program — the company builds and ramps its own facilities rather than acquiring them — converting capital expenditure into long-dated, high-margin licensed capacity.

A segment revenue breakdown was not available for this issuer; see the latest annual report for business-line detail. Geographic revenue breakdown was likewise not available. On the consolidated basis that is reported, trailing-twelve-month revenue reached $6,206.1 million against full-year 2025 revenue of $5,935.2 million, with TTM net income of $621.0 million and FY2025 net income of $566.2 million — a franchise that has scaled revenue at roughly 10.9% compounded over four years while holding gross margin near 42.5% and EBITDA margin near 23.7%.

The durable moat rests on scale, local density and regulatory friction. As the largest operator, EHC holds referral relationships across acute-care hospitals and case-management networks, spreads shared clinical and administrative infrastructure across a national footprint, and operates under certificate-of-need and licensing regimes that restrict de novo entry in many states. The balance sheet — $7,457.5 million of assets against $3,996.4 million of liabilities and $2,597.7 million of equity — funds that build program without balance-sheet stress.
thesis.competitor_analysis: Encompass Health competes in a structurally fragmented post-acute rehabilitation market alongside other inpatient rehabilitation operators and the rehabilitation units of large diversified acute-care hospital chains; no peer valuation multiples were supplied in this dataset, so relative positioning is described qualitatively rather than through a peer-multiple table. On the evidence available, EHC's own trading multiple of 10.8x EV/EBITDA sits essentially on its five-year median of 10.6x — a 'fair' classification — and its 20.3x P/E is carried by a 10.5% FY2025 revenue growth rate and a 23.7% EBITDA margin rather than by any scarcity premium. Versus smaller rehabilitation operators, the differentiator is scale plus a self-funded de novo pipeline that adds capacity at controlled cost and defends local referral density; versus the diversified hospital chains, EHC offers pure-play rehabilitation exposure with markedly lower balance-sheet leverage ($3,996.4 million of liabilities against $7,457.5 million of assets). Absent peer multiples, the competitive conclusion is that EHC's multiple is fair rather than a relative discount — the investment case rests on the DCF gap to $151.37, not on peer-relative mispricing.

thesis.narrative:
Encompass Health enters this initiation at $124.36 against a DCF-anchored fair value of $151.37 — an implied +21.7% gap — yet the call is Hold, not Buy, because that anchor is a single discounted-cash-flow method with no cross-validation. The DCF's own band spans $151.37 to $151.37 before publication widening, and the published range of $113.53 to $189.22 is wide enough that the current price sits comfortably inside it. The base case itself is credible on the supplied fundamentals: revenue compounded at 10.9% over four years to $5,935.2 million in FY2025 and $6,206.1 million on a trailing-twelve-month basis, with TTM net income of $621.0 million and an EBITDA margin near 23.7%.

The market's own arithmetic is the reality check. Holding the model's 6.97% WACC fixed, $124.36 embeds 5.29% flat perpetual growth over a ten-year horizon — above the 3.0% terminal assumption but below the 10.9% trailing CAGR, so the gap between price and fair value is a question of fade speed, not of an implausible market forecast. Holding the growth fade fixed, the market implies a 7.49% discount rate, roughly 52bp above the model's 6.97% WACC. Momentum is supportive but leaves no cushion: the shares are +3.3% over one year, sit at 92% of the 52-week range, and are only -2.3% off the high, so the de novo growth story has already been re-rated.

What holds the recommendation at Hold is the flow evidence combined with the single-method risk. Insiders were net sellers of $151.37 over the past 90 days with zero open-market purchases, led by CEO Mark J Tarr's $151.37 sale — a distribution pattern, not accumulation, that argues management sees the shares near fair value. Reported 13F coverage is only 7.3% of shares outstanding, so holder concentration cannot be asserted from an incomplete index. With EV/EBITDA at 10.8x against a five-year median of 10.6x, the stock trades at fair, and a +21.7% DCF gap is not large enough relative to the method's own error band to justify a Buy.
thesis.news_summary: The last 30 days of news flow are unambiguously constructive, with the catalyst feed scoring net sentiment of +1.15 and every high-impact item positive. Five product-launch events dominate the tape: the opening of a new inpatient rehabilitation hospital in Bangor, Maine, a new hospital in Lower Providence, Pennsylvania, and the company's first small-format hospital alongside a replacement facility in Montgomery County, Texas — each carrying an impact score of 3 and reinforcing the de novo capacity engine that underwrites the 10.9% historical growth rate. A sell-side upgrade to Buy in late September 2026 adds a third-party validation point, and the company's own 8-K filings provide primary-source confirmation of the capacity and financing activity. This flow supports the growth leg of the thesis, but it also explains why the shares sit at 92% of their 52-week range with a +3.3% one-year return — the market has already paid for the pipeline. News sentiment therefore corroborates the DCF's $151.37 fair value while doing nothing to close the +21.7% gap to it, consistent with a Hold.

thesis.valuation_overview:
The valuation rests on a single discounted-cash-flow method; no second method was included in the synthesis, so there is no cross-validation and the confidence tier is medium. The DCF discounts ten years of explicit free cash flow at a 6.97% WACC, fading revenue growth from the 10.9% four-year CAGR toward a 3.0% terminal rate, and produces an implied price of $151.37 against a ±20% placeholder band of $151.37 to $151.37, widened for publication to $113.53–$189.22.

That method carries a data-quality weight of 0.85 in the blend, and with only one contributor the weighted output equals the DCF mid: $151.37, or +21.7% versus the $124.36 market price. The divergence between the DCF and the market is best read through the reverse-DCF: holding the growth fade fixed, $124.36 implies a 7.49% discount rate, above the model's 6.97%; holding WACC fixed, it implies 5.29% flat perpetual growth, above the 3.0% terminal rate but well below the 10.9% historical CAGR. The market is therefore not pricing an implausible outcome — which is precisely why a medium-confidence, single-method anchor supports Hold rather than Buy, and why the subject's own 10.8x EV/EBITDA, essentially on its five-year median of 10.6x, reads as fair rather than as a discount to fair value.
